title: #74 Ask an Impossible Question to Further Check Students' Understanding
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton describes a Year 8 maths lesson where a teacher deliberately posed a question -- finding the area of a triangle using trigonometry students hadn't yet been taught -- that was genuinely unanswerable with the tools available to them. He argues the impossibility itself was the point: presented without any softening, the question functioned as a clean check for understanding, since students had to reveal, unprompted, whether they recognised the limits of what they currently knew. He connects this to an earlier point he's made about hints undermining diagnostic validity -- signalling that a question is unusual robs students of the chance to demonstrate, unaided, what they actually know or don't know. The teacher's subsequent mini-whiteboard check, run without any hint that the question was a trap, surfaced genuine misconceptions that a softened version of the same question likely would have masked. Barton's takeaway is a recommendation to occasionally include a deliberately impossible question in a sequence of checks, but only if its impossibility is disguised rather than flagged.
points: The diagnostic value of an "impossible" question depends entirely on withholding any signal that it's unusual -- hints like "think carefully about this one" reduce the question's validity as a check for understanding.
Presenting an unanswerable question exactly like every other question in the sequence forces students to reveal, unprompted, whether they recognise the limits of their own knowledge.

Barton connects this tip explicitly to his earlier writing on the problem with unavoidable hints, treating disguised difficulty as part of a broader principle about protecting the reliability of checks for understanding.
The technique surfaced real, specific misconceptions in the observed lesson precisely because the teacher offered no verbal or tonal cue that anything about the question was different.
quotes: The students will not be taught trigonometry for a few years, so the question was impossible to answer with the tools at their disposal. And that is what made it such a good check for understanding.
The teacher made this even more effective by not saying anything. She just popped it up on the board, just like she had done for every other question that lesson.
I have seen teachers use similar unanswerable questions, but sugar-coat them with hints such as Think carefully about this one, or Are we sure we can answer this one?

I have written previously about the problem with offering unavoidable hints - they reduce the validity of the check for understanding, and rob students of the opportunity to think hard and show what they really can do.
By offering no such hints, the teacher had an accurate sense of what students knew and didn't know, and the subsequent mini-whiteboard check dew out some interesting misconceptions.
So, now and then, throw in an impossible question, but disguise the fact that it is impossible.
